newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's main opposition party sets sights on power.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's main opposition party sets sights on power.

text.p: Heady from last week's big gains in two state elections, Mexico's main opposition party on Sunday mapped out its strategy for ousting the party that has ruled Mexico for 67 consecutive years.
In a two-day party convention that ended on Sunday, the conservative National Action Party (PAN) took direct aim at the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

"With this debate over our electoral platform, we begin the path to victory in the 1997 (Congressional) elections, and we're going for the presidency of the republic in 2000," PAN President Felipe Calderon Hinojosa told 7,000 delegates at a sports arena, to a roar of applause.

The PAN has come to rule over 37 percent of the Mexican population through four governorships and 247 mayoral posts, whetting its appetite for more in Congressional elections next year as it threatens to end the PRI's longstanding majority.

Polls put the PAN way ahead in the first-ever race for Mexico City governor to be held along with the Congressional vote next July. In the past the president of the country has appointed a regent, or mayor.
The loudest cheers of the convention came on Saturday when PAN's Mexico City chief Gonzalo Altamirano declared, "We're going for Mexico City in 1997."

Judging from the crowd's cheers, delegates appeared to favour Diego Fernandez Cevallos as their candidate for Mexico City. Polls show Fernandez, the PAN's losing presidential candidate in 1994, as the clear front-runner, but Fernandez has said that he is not interested.
In local elections last week in the state of Mexico, which surrounds Mexico City, the PAN won many of the mayoral posts in the largest cities in the capital's surburbs.
The PAN also posted big gains in northern Coahuila state along the border with Texas, although the PRI was dominant in rural Hidalgo state near Mexico City.
The leftist Democratic Revolution Party (PRD), which showed solid gains in last Sunday's local elections, is also angling for power.

However pollsters say the PRI is far from dead and has a good chance of keeping its majority in Congress despite the decline in its political fortunes linked to the economic crisis which followed the December 1994 peso devaluation.
A series of embarrassing corruption scandals has also dented the PRI's image.

Calderon predicted that the PAN was close to becoming Mexico's top party, saying, "The country doesn't need to start a political transition. It's already happening. What is urgently needed to is finish it."

At the convention, the party approved a legislative platform for the next three years that proposes radical changes in Mexican politics. The PAN's presidential candidate is expected to run on a similar platform in 2000.

On the economic front, it proposes slashing taxes and eliminating government departments, replacing the current "paternalistic, omnipresent and omnipotent" government with a "jointly shared and subsidiary" one.

"It's necessary to change the view of the financial indicators to indicators that affect the microeconomy, families and businesses, and not just what occurs on a macreconomic level," the platform said.
Politically, the PAN calls for decentralizing power and bolstering the budgets and authority of states and cities.
On social issues, the PAN toed a conservative line, echoing the positions of the Catholic Churh on abortion and the family.
